description: Hi! I'm the founder of Vibe Orbits, a solo team building fast with AI-assisted coding. I turn ideas into working prototypes quickly, and I'm looking for teammates who bring what I don't: data analysis, data visualization, clear writing for the pitch, and video for the demo. Beginners welcome, just bring curiosity about space and a willingness to build something great. Join me and let's launch something unforgettable!
summary:
What we developed. Mars Outpost Trainer is a free browser game, playable on any phone or laptop with no install, in which students aged 12 to 16 command a four-person Mars outpost through three missions.

How it addresses the challenge. Each mission gives a cargo budget that cannot buy everything. Players place habitat, solar, battery, oxygen, greenhouse and radiation-wall modules on a 3D site while live arrows show what the next sol will do to power, oxygen, food and crew health. Dust storms cut solar output, and a radiation wall shields only the tiles it touches, so placement is the decision. Every failure is traced to a choice in the debrief.

Why it matters. It makes real mission trade-offs tangible and fun, backed by sourced NASA facts and a quiz after every mission.
details:
What it does. The player is the outpost commander. Every sol (Martian day, 24 h 39 min) has two halves: plan, then run. In the plan half the player places, moves or removes modules on an 8 by 8 grid with rocky and ice tiles. Four meters show power, oxygen, food and crew health, and beside each meter a live arrow shows exactly what the next sol will add or take away. In the run half the Sun crosses the sky, night falls, and the meters move. A sol report lists what was made and used. After the last sol a debrief shows a sol-by-sol table and one sentence that names the decision behind the result, for example: “The blackout on sol 3 stopped your oxygen makers.”

The trade-offs. Cargo is the constraint. In Mission 1 a crew of four breathes 12 oxygen a sol and one Oxygen Maker makes 7, so one maker is not enough, but two makers plus the power to run them do not fit in 12 cargo without draining the battery. Mission 2 adds food and a two-sol dust storm that cuts solar output to a quarter, so the player must choose between a greenhouse and a battery. Mission 3 adds solar storms; a Radiation Wall protects only the four tiles touching it, so a wall on the far side of the grid does nothing. Every mechanic forces an either/or choice that the arrows make visible before the player commits.

How it is built. One HTML file: Three.js for the 3D scene (low-poly, toon-shaded, drops to low quality on slow phones), a small deterministic simulation (a pure function; the same code drives the preview arrows and the real sol), Web Audio for sounds, no server and no accounts. Works with touch, mouse and keyboard, respects reduced-motion settings, and labels every control for screen readers. Progress and preferences are saved in the browser only.

Who it is for. Middle and early high-school students, played alone or on a classroom projector. A first-play tutorial from Nova, the guide character, takes under a minute. Teachers can use the Science & sources screen in the missions menu to see which real missions each fact comes from and which simplifications the game makes.

Creativity and factors considered. Placement is part of the trade-off, so the 3D grid is gameplay rather than decoration. Cost: free, no install, runs on low-end phones. Accessibility: keyboard play, screen-reader labels, reduced motion, colour never used alone to carry meaning. Energy: the game’s own theme; blackouts stop life support, as they would on Mars.

What we would add next. A water loop with ice-tile extractors, a Moon mode with 14-day nights, random event decks, Urdu and other languages, and a classroom mode where a teacher sees every student’s debrief.
